terms.def: The way radio waves travel from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna.
terms.more: Signals can travel in a straight line, by reflection, by bending in the atmosphere or by way of the ionosphere. Which one applies depends mostly on frequency.

terms.def: A signal reaching the receiver by more than one route at the same time, for example directly and by bouncing off buildings or hills.
terms.more: The copies cancel in some spots and reinforce in others, so VHF strength can change when an antenna moves a few feet. It causes picket fencing on mobile signals and is likely to raise error rates on data.

terms.def: Rapid flutter heard on the signal of a moving station.
terms.more: It is caused by multipath propagation: the vehicle passes quickly through spots where the signal copies cancel and spots where they reinforce.

terms.def: A received signal getting weaker and stronger over time.
terms.more: Irregular fading of signals that come by way of the ionosphere is likely caused by random combining of signals arriving via different paths.

terms.def: How strong a radio signal is when it arrives at the receiver.
terms.more: Multipath can make VHF signal strength vary greatly over a few feet. Cross-polarized antennas on a line-of-sight path reduce received signal strength.

terms.def: The loss of radio signal energy as it is soaked up by something in its path.
terms.more: Vegetation absorbs UHF and microwave signals, which leads to poor reception of weak signals.

terms.def: Water falling from the sky, such as rain or snow.
terms.more: Precipitation might decrease range at microwave frequencies. Fog or rain has little effect on 10-meter and 6-meter band signals.

terms.def: Radio waves of very high frequency and very short wavelength, above the UHF range.
terms.more: Vegetation absorbs microwave signals, and precipitation might decrease their range.

terms.def: The direction in which the electric field of a radio wave points, such as vertical or horizontal.
terms.more: It is defined by the orientation of the electric field, not the magnetic field. An antenna with vertical elements produces a vertically polarized wave.

terms.def: A radio wave whose electric field is parallel to the ground, as made by an antenna with elements parallel to the ground.
terms.more: Horizontal polarization is normally used for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands.

terms.def: A radio wave whose electric field is at right angles to the ground, as made by an antenna with upright elements.
terms.more: Signals returned by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized, so either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for them.

terms.def: A mismatch where the receiving antenna is oriented differently from the wave's polarization, for example one antenna vertical and the other horizontal.
terms.more: Over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path, cross-polarization reduces the received signal strength.

terms.def: A wave whose electric field keeps turning instead of holding one direction, giving a changing mix of vertical and horizontal.
terms.more: Signals propagated by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized, so either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception.

terms.def: Continuous wave: Morse code sent by switching a radio signal on and off.
terms.more: Long-distance CW contacts on the VHF and UHF bands normally use horizontal antenna polarization.

terms.def: Single sideband: a voice mode that uses less bandwidth than FM and works well for weak signals.
terms.more: Long-distance SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands normally use horizontal antenna polarization.

terms.def: A straight, unblocked path between the transmitting antenna and the receiving antenna.
terms.more: On a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path the antennas should have the same polarization. If the direct path is blocked, a reflected path may still work.

terms.def: A radio wave bouncing off something, such as a building or a hill, and continuing in a new direction.
terms.more: If obstructions block the direct path to a repeater, try to find a path that reflects your signal to it. The ionosphere can reflect HF radio waves.

terms.def: An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction instead of sending them equally all around.
terms.more: With a directional antenna you can aim at a surface that reflects your signal to a repeater when the direct path is blocked.

terms.def: A station that receives a signal and retransmits it at the same time, usually from a high location, to extend the range of other stations.
terms.more: If buildings block the direct path to a distant repeater, a directional antenna may reach it by a reflected path.

terms.def: How often the pieces of a data transmission are received wrongly.
terms.more: Multipath propagation is likely to increase error rates on data transmissions.

terms.def: The upper region of the atmosphere, electrically charged by the Sun, that can return radio waves to Earth.
terms.more: It can reflect HF radio waves, so long-distance contacts are far more common on HF. UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere.

terms.def: A high region of the ionosphere that returns radio signals to Earth over long distances.
terms.more: At the peak of the sunspot cycle it may carry 6 and 10 meter signals long distances. The best time on 10 meters is from dawn to shortly after sunset during high sunspot activity.

terms.def: The regular rise and fall in the number of dark spots on the Sun, which shows how active the Sun is.
terms.more: High sunspot activity strengthens the F region. During the peak of the cycle, 6 and 10 meters may provide long-distance communication.

terms.def: A wave made of an electric field and a magnetic field travelling together through space. Radio waves and light are both this kind of wave.
terms.more: The two fields are at right angles to each other. In free space all radio waves travel at the speed of light, whatever their frequency.

terms.def: One of the two components of a radio wave; the invisible force that acts on electric charges.
terms.more: It is at right angles to the magnetic field. The orientation of the electric field defines the wave's polarization.

terms.def: One of the two components of a radio wave; the invisible force that acts on magnets and moving charges.
terms.more: It is at right angles to the electric field. It is not the field used to name the wave's polarization.

terms.def: Empty space with nothing in the way to slow or block a radio wave.
terms.more: In free space every radio wave travels at the speed of light, about 300,000,000 meters per second, whatever its frequency.

terms.def: The speed at which light and radio waves travel through free space.
terms.more: It is approximately 300,000,000 meters per second. All radio frequencies travel at this same velocity in free space.

terms.def: The distance a radio wave travels during one complete cycle.
terms.more: Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases. Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz. Amateur bands are identified by their approximate wavelength in meters.

terms.def: The number of complete cycles a radio wave makes each second, measured in hertz.
terms.more: As frequency increases, wavelength gets shorter. Frequency does not change the speed of the wave in free space.

terms.def: Megahertz: a unit of frequency equal to one million hertz, or one million cycles per second.
terms.more: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz. HF is 3 to 30 MHz, VHF is 30 to 300 MHz and UHF is 300 to 3000 MHz.

terms.def: A range of frequencies set aside for a particular use, such as amateur radio.
terms.more: Amateur bands are identified by frequency and also by their approximate wavelength in meters, for example the 2-meter band.

terms.def: High frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 3 to 30 MHz.
terms.more: Long-distance propagation by the ionosphere is far more common on HF than on VHF and higher frequencies.

terms.def: Very high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 30 MHz to 300 MHz.
terms.more: It is the range just above HF and just below UHF. VHF signals normally travel a little beyond line of sight, to the radio horizon.

terms.def: Ultra high frequency: the part of the radio spectrum from 300 to 3000 MHz.
terms.more: It is the range just above VHF. UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere, so simplex UHF signals are rarely heard beyond the radio horizon.

terms.def: The amateur band with a wavelength of about 10 meters, at the top of the HF range.
terms.more: Best for long distance via the F region from dawn to shortly after sunset during high sunspot activity. Sporadic E can also bring strong signals. Fog or rain has little effect.

terms.def: The amateur band with a wavelength of about 6 meters, at the bottom of the VHF range.
terms.more: It is the band best suited to meteor scatter. It can open by sporadic E, and by the F region during the peak of the sunspot cycle. Fog or rain has little effect.

terms.def: The amateur VHF band with a wavelength of about 2 meters.
terms.more: Sporadic E is the propagation most commonly associated with occasional strong 2-meter signals from beyond the radio horizon.

terms.def: The distance at which the curve of the Earth blocks direct radio signals between two stations.
terms.more: For VHF and UHF it is more distant than the visual horizon, because the atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly. Simplex UHF signals are rarely heard beyond it.

terms.def: Communicating directly from one station to another, without a repeater.
terms.more: Simplex UHF signals are rarely heard beyond their radio horizon because UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere.

terms.def: The bending of a radio wave as it passes through the atmosphere.
terms.more: The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly, which is why the radio horizon for VHF and UHF signals is more distant than the visual horizon.

terms.def: VHF signals reflected from an aurora, the glowing curtain of charged particles seen in the sky toward the poles.
terms.more: Signals received this way are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound.

terms.def: Propagation by occasional dense patches of charged gas in the E region of the ionosphere.
terms.more: It is the type most commonly associated with occasional strong signals on the 10-, 6- and 2-meter bands from beyond the radio horizon.

terms.def: The bending of radio waves over a sharp edge, such as a ridge or the edge of a building.
terms.more: It may allow signals to travel beyond obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations.

terms.def: VHF and UHF signals being trapped and guided along the Earth by layers of air in the troposphere, the lowest part of the atmosphere.
terms.more: It allows over-the-horizon VHF and UHF contacts to about 300 miles on a regular basis. It is caused by temperature inversions in the atmosphere.

terms.def: A weather condition where a layer of warm air sits above cooler air, the reverse of the normal arrangement.
terms.more: Temperature inversions in the atmosphere cause tropospheric ducting.

terms.def: Communication by reflecting signals off the short-lived trails of charged gas left by meteors burning up in the atmosphere.
terms.more: The 6-meter band is best suited for meteor scatter.
